h1: Answering 'have you worked on SEO?' in an interview
metaTitle: “Have You Worked on SEO?” How to Answer It
metaDescription: A 90-second structure for answering the SEO experience question, with three worked scripts: no experience, a side project, and agency team work.
answer: Answer in about 90 seconds using five beats: scope, constraint, what you did, what moved against a baseline, and what you'd change. Say yes only if you can name a site, a query and a number. If you've never done it professionally, say so plainly and describe your own project instead.
takeaways: It isn't a yes/no question. It tests whether you can tell a **causal story with a number attached** — and whether you'll overclaim.
Ninety seconds. Longer and they stop listening; shorter and you've said nothing checkable.
"Not professionally, but here's what I've run myself" is a strong answer. A vague yes is a weak one.
Never cite a percentage without the absolute underneath it. 300% of forty visits is a hundred and twenty visits.

sections.h2: What the question is actually testing
body: Nobody asks "have you worked on SEO?" expecting yes or no. They're testing three things, and none is your knowledge of ranking factors.

First, whether you can describe cause and effect. SEO attracts people who were standing nearby when something improved and aren't sure why. The interviewer wants to know if you can separate what you did from what happened around you.
Second, whether you'll overclaim. The fastest way to lose a senior interviewer is a number you can't source.

Third, whether you're pleasant to correct. Most SEO work is being wrong on Tuesday and adjusting by Thursday, so a candidate who describes a mistake calmly interviews far better than one whose every project succeeded.
Five beats. Practise it out loud twice and it stops sounding rehearsed. The timings are a guide — the ratio is the point.

table.caption: A five-beat answer that fits inside ninety seconds.
head: Beat
Roughly
What goes in it
rows: The site, its size, its market. "A 40-page B2B site selling into the UAE" says more than "a client project".
What made it hard: no dev time, no budget, a legacy CMS, four hours a week. Constraints make a story credible.
Two or three specific actions, in order, with the reason for that order. Not everything you touched.
The number, the baseline it moved from, the date range, the source.
One thing you got wrong and what you'd do instead. The beat candidates skip and interviewers remember.

callout.title: Why the baseline beat matters
callout.body: Serious SEO people judge work against a frozen starting number, not a rising line. It's how our own guarantee works — a client's trailing-90-day organic leads, frozen on day one. Talk that way and you sound like someone who's been held to a number. See [how that works](/seo).

sections.h2: Script 1 — you have no professional experience
body: Lead with the truth. Inflating a college assignment into client work fails on the second follow-up. The script, with your details in brackets:
bullets: "**Not professionally — I'll be straight about that.** What I have done is run my own site since [month]. Twelve pages about [topic], all mine."
"**The constraint was no audience and no links**, so I targeted queries where the top ten was weak — old forum threads, posts that dodged the question."
"**I set up Search Console on day one and screenshotted the empty graph**, so I have a real baseline. Then a pillar page, a cluster, internal links done properly."
"**Between [month] and [month] those pages went from zero to about [N] impressions a week**, and I'm on page one for [exact query]. You can check it."
"**What I got wrong was indexing.** Twenty pages published, twelve indexed, for two months — a stray `robots.txt` rule. I found it in the Pages report and now I check indexation before publishing."

callout.title: Don't do this
callout.body: "I've done SEO for a few clients" when you helped a cousin's shop once. They'll ask which clients, which vertical, over what period, and the recovery is worse than never claiming it. Build the [90-day portfolio project](/answers/how-hard-is-it-to-get-into-an-seo-career) and you'll never need the lie.

sections.h2: Script 2 — a side project or your own site
body: Stronger ground than most candidates realise. On a site you own outright you made every decision and can explain every one. Lean into the constraint, too: four hours a week is a good story, because prioritising under scarcity is the skill being hired.
numbered: **Scope:** "I run [site], a [topic] site doing roughly [N] visits a month from search. Every decision on it is mine, including the bad ones."
**Constraint:** "Four hours a week, no budget past hosting. That forced me to be selective rather than thorough."
**What you did:** "The biggest change was consolidation. I had [N] pages competing for one query, so none ranked. I merged them, redirected the rest and rewrote the survivor to answer the question."
**What moved:** "Clicks on that cluster went from [x] to [y] between [month] and [month], average position from [x] to [y]. Search Console, not an estimate."
**What you'd change:** "I'd fix the technical problems first. I spent six weeks writing on a site that couldn't index new pages."

sections.h2: Script 3 — you worked on a team
body: The failure mode here is the opposite of script 1: claiming the team's number as your own. Every interviewer listens for it. Be specific about your slice and generous about everyone else's — it reads as senior, not modest.
bullets: "**I was one of four on a [industry] account** — a strategist, a technical SEO, a writer and me. I owned on-page and internal linking for [section]."
"**The constraint was engineering time.** Their dev team shipped one template change a quarter, so we front-loaded everything doable inside the CMS."
"**Over two quarters that section went from [x] to [y] non-brand clicks a month.** I can't claim that whole number — the technical fix in month one probably did more than my content work."
"**My part was [x]:** I rebuilt internal linking across [N] pages and rewrote the [N] titles with impressions but no clicks. That's where I'd start again."
"**What I'd change:** I didn't push hard enough for the second template fix. I'd make the case in rupees next time."

sections.h2: Numbers to cite, and numbers to avoid
body: One credible number beats four impressive ones. Every figure should survive "where did that come from?"

bullets: **Non-brand clicks and impressions from Search Console**, with the date range. First-party data, and they know it.
**Average position for named queries** — see [average position](/glossary/average-position) — not a site-wide average.
**Indexed pages versus published pages.** A quietly excellent detail: it shows you check.
**Leads or revenue from organic**, if you genuinely had CRM access. This one ends the conversation in your favour.
**Percentage and absolute together.** "Up 140%, from 320 to 770 clicks a month."
**A percentage with no base.** "Grew traffic 300%" invites "from what to what?", and the answer is often forty visits.
**"Ranked number one on Google"** with no query, date or location. Rankings are personalised and volatile; stating one flatly says you don't know that.
**Domain Authority or Domain Rating as an achievement.** Third-party scores, and using one as a result marks you as someone who reports what's easy to measure.
**Third-party traffic estimates presented as fact**, when Search Console was available.
**Anything from a job you can't discuss.** Under NDA, say so and describe the method instead.

body: A good ninety-second answer buys you the rest of the interview. These follow it near-universally.
numbered: **"How do you know it was your work and not seasonality or a core update?"** Honesty wins: often you can't be certain, but here's how you'd narrow it — compare unaffected sections, check dates against known rollouts, see if competitors moved.
**"Where exactly did that number come from?"** Name the tool, the report, the date range. Hesitation undoes everything before it.
**"What would you do with ten times the budget?"** Testing prioritisation, not ambition. "More content" scores badly; naming the constraint you'd remove scores well.
**"What didn't work?"** Have a second failure ready. The one you volunteered doesn't count twice.

**"How would you approach our site?"** The question that decides it. Spend twenty minutes beforehand: a `site:` search to sanity-check indexation, a skim of their titles, one page through PageSpeed Insights. Arrive with one specific, non-insulting observation. Almost nobody does, and it beats any rehearsed line about [what the daily job involves](/answers/what-does-an-seo-specialist-do).

faqs.q: What if I genuinely have no SEO experience at all?
faqs.a: Say so in the first five seconds, then pivot to what you've built. "Not professionally, but I've run my own site for four months and here's what happened" is a good answer. What kills the interview isn't inexperience — it's a vague yes that collapses under one follow-up question.

faqs.q: Should I bring a portfolio or case study to an SEO interview?
faqs.a: Yes, and keep it to one page. Baseline screenshot with a date, the queries you targeted, a dated change log, what moved, what didn't. Send the link in your application too — most candidates don't, and it's the single fastest way to get a CV read properly.

faqs.q: How long should my answer be?
faqs.a: Around ninety seconds. Long enough for scope, constraint, action, result and reflection; short enough that they interrupt with a follow-up rather than checking the clock. If you're routinely running past two minutes, you're listing tasks instead of telling one story.

faqs.q: Is it risky to admit a mistake in an interview?
faqs.a: Far less risky than claiming a flawless record. Interviewers who've done the job know every SEO project contains at least one bad call. Pick a mistake with a clean diagnosis and a fix — an indexing error, a redirect you got wrong — not a judgement failure like ignoring a brief.

faqs.q: What if the interviewer asks about a tool I've never used?
faqs.a: Say you haven't used it, name the closest thing you have used, and describe what you'd do with it. "I've used Screaming Frog rather than Sitebulb, but the crawl I'd run is the same and here's what I'd look at first." Bluffing about a tool fails within two questions.
